newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel reaffirms no EMU if deficit limit missed.
newsitem.headline: Waigel reaffirms no EMU if deficit limit missed.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel reaffirmed in an interview released on Saturday that strict fulfilment of the Maastricht criteria must take precedence over the scheduled 1999 start of the EU single currency.

But Waigel said Germany was determined to ensure that its 1997 public deficit was below three percent of GDP, the reference value set down in the Maastricht treaty as one of the criteria for joining European monetary union (EMU).
And he said Germany was sticking to its insistence that three percent meant 3.0 percent, and not a fraction more.

The Bild am Sonntag newspaper asked Waigel what he thought of the opinion of economic institutes which say the "euro" can still be introduced if member countries' public deficits are slightly above three percent of gross domestic product.
"I'm sticking to what I have said. We have to achieve the three percent. 3.0 means 3.0," he replied, according to an advance release from Sunday's edition.
"Anything else would harm the credibility and public acceptance of the euro," he said.

Most experts expect Germany to miss the target and record a deficit of around 3.2 percent of GDP because of the heavy burden of mass unemployment. Tax revenue estimates to be released next month are likely to shed more light on the matter.
Asked what would happen if Germany did not make the criteria, Waigel replied: "The incontrovertible principle still applies. The timetable is dictated by economic convergence."
